messages.content: What is an IDO in SyteLine?

An IDO (Intelligent Data Object) is the smart business layer of SyteLine. It is a flattened property view over one or more base SQL tables, and all application-database access goes through IDOs via the IDO runtime service. Think of it this way: Forms are the UI, IDOs are the business logic and data access, and Application Event Handlers hold business-process logic.
What are the core operations I can call on an IDO?

The core IDO operations are LoadCollection, UpdateCollection, and Invoke, plus OpenSession for session management. LoadCollection reads records, UpdateCollection writes them back, and Invoke calls IDO methods. Everything flows through the IDO runtime service — application code never touches the SQL tables directly.
What is FormSync and why does it matter for customizations?

FormSync merges your customizations with the vendor's form definitions at upgrade time. Custom metadata is kept separate from the base application, so when Infor ships a new version, FormSync reconciles your changes against the new base forms instead of overwriting them. That separation is what makes SyteLine upgrades survivable for customized tenants.
Where does business logic live in SyteLine — forms, IDOs, or somewhere else?

All three layers have a job. Forms are the UI. IDOs are the smart business layer — the flattened property view over the SQL tables that every data access goes through. Business-process logic lives in Application Event Handlers. If you are debugging behavior, check the event handlers; if you are debugging data access, check the IDO.
Which IDO names are officially documented for customers and orders?

The officially documented ones I will stand behind are SLCustomers for customers and SLCos for customer-order headers. Names like SLItems, SLCoitems, SLPOs, SLPoItems, SLJobs, SLJobRoutes, SLJobmatls, and SLLocations are community-corroborated — widely used, but confirm them against IdoCollections and IdoProperties on your live tenant before treating them as ground truth.
How do I verify an IDO name on my tenant instead of trusting a list?

Introspect the tenant itself: query IdoCollections and IdoProperties on the live system. Community lists are a starting point, not ground truth — tenant configuration, versions, and customizations vary. If the IDO is not in IdoCollections on your tenant, it does not exist there no matter what a list says.
What does it mean that Mongoose is a metadata-driven platform?

It means application behavior is defined in metadata — form definitions, IDO definitions, and event handlers — rather than in compiled code. Your customizations live as metadata kept separate from the base application, which is exactly why FormSync can merge them at upgrade time. When something behaves oddly, the metadata is the first place to look.
Can I just query the SQL tables directly for a report?

In the product itself, no — all application-database access goes through IDOs via the IDO runtime service. That is the architecture, not a suggestion. For analytics outside the application you would work from replicated or warehoused data, but anything the application does flows through the IDO layer, which is where business rules and security are enforced.
An IDO is described as a flattened property view. What does that mean in practice?

It means one IDO can surface properties drawn from several underlying SQL tables as if they were a single flat record. You work with the IDO's properties — the flattened view — and the IDO runtime handles mapping them back to the base tables on LoadCollection and UpdateCollection. You do not need to know the joins; the IDO owns them.
In multi-site SyteLine, why do some table names end in _all?

The _all suffix marks multi-site replication views. The base tables drop the suffix. So when you see a view named like co_mst_all, you are looking at the replicated multi-site view; the base table is co_mst. Spelling matters here — it is matltran, not matltrans.
What are the key SQL tables for customers and customer orders?

customer_mst for the customer master, co_mst for order headers (key fields co_num and cust_po), and coitem_mst for order lines. The line table carries co_num, item, u_m, stat, due_date, promise_date, release_date, qty_ordered, and cust_po. Learn those three tables cold — most order diagnostics start there.
What are the key purchasing tables in SyteLine?

po_mst for PO headers (po_num) and poitem_mst for PO lines. The line table carries po_release, item, due_date, prom_date, qty_ordered_conf, unit_cost_conv, and stat. Note that due_date and prom_date are separate fields on the line — never conflate them.
What are the key inventory tables?

The item master (item), itemwhse for the per-site item record, matltran for every material transaction — that is the audit trail — and the lot/serial masters. If inventory numbers look wrong, matltran is where you reconstruct what actually happened.
What are the key manufacturing tables?

job for job headers, jobmatl for job materials, jobroute for operations, and jobtran as the labor transaction audit trail. The jobmatl table is the workhorse: job, suffix, sequence, item, oper_num, matl_qty, qty_released, qty_issued, u_m, scrap_fact, backflush, bflush_loc, matl_type.
Is it matltran or matltrans?

It is matltran — no trailing s. Every material transaction lands there, making it the audit trail for inventory movement. Getting the spelling right matters when you are naming it in front of a planner who has used SyteLine for twenty years.
What is the itemwhse table?

itemwhse is the per-site item record — the item master (item) holds the global definition, and itemwhse holds the site-specific side: quantities, costing, and planning parameters for that site. In a multi-site tenant, availability questions are answered at the itemwhse level, not the item level.
What fields on jobmatl matter most for a materials investigation?

job, suffix, and sequence identify the record; item and oper_num tie it to the material and operation; matl_qty, qty_released, and qty_issued tell you planned versus released versus actually issued; u_m is the unit of measure; scrap_fact is the scrap multiplier; backflush and bflush_loc control backflushing; matl_type classifies the material. qty_issued versus matl_qty is usually where the story is.
What fields does coitem_mst carry on an order line?

co_num, item, u_m, stat, due_date, promise_date, release_date, qty_ordered, and cust_po. The three dates are separate fields — when promise_date is blank, due date is used. stat is load-bearing: the Scheduler and APS interpret the line by its status code.
What is jobtran used for?

jobtran is the labor transaction audit trail — it records labor against jobs, production schedules, JIT, and work centers. When labor cost or reported hours look wrong, jobtran is the record of what was actually reported, the same way matltran is the record for material.
What is the difference between due_date and prom_date on a PO line?

They are separate fields on poitem_mst and they mean different things: due_date is when you need it, prom_date is when the supplier promised it. A line can be due Friday with a promise date of next Tuesday — that gap is exactly the kind of thing that makes an order late. Never conflate them.
What is qty_ordered_conf on a PO line?

It is the confirmed quantity ordered on the PO line (poitem_mst). Compare it against quantity actually received: if qty ordered is greater than qty received, the status is O, and the due date is past, you are looking at the community-reported Past Due pattern — verify the exact field semantics on your tenant.
What does unit_cost_conv mean on poitem_mst?

It is the converted unit cost on the PO line — the cost expressed in the relevant currency after conversion. Costing questions on purchased material start there, alongside qty_ordered_conf for the quantity side.
What are the customer order line statuses and what do they mean?

Planned, then Ordered/Open, then Complete at the header. Planned lines do not update the customer's On Order Balance. Switching a line from Planned to Ordered fires the credit check and starts updating balances. Blanket lines follow Planned, Ordered, Complete. Statuses are load-bearing — the Scheduler and APS read them as instructions, not labels.
Why does a Planned order line not affect the On Order Balance?

Because Planned means the demand is recognized but not committed. The On Order Balance only accumulates Ordered/Open lines — that is the balance the credit check enforces against. This is also why exceeding the credit limit saves a line as Planned instead of Ordered: the system refuses to commit demand it cannot extend credit for.
What happens when I switch a customer order line from Planned to Ordered?

Two things fire: the credit check runs against the customer, and the line starts updating the On Order Balance. If the customer is over their limit, the line drops back to Planned — that is the credit hold expressing itself as a status, not as an error message.
What are the P and O status codes I see in the database on order lines?

The community mapping is P = Planned and O = Ordered — but treat that as unverified on your tenant until you confirm it. Status codes are exactly the kind of thing that varies by configuration, so check a known line on the form, note its displayed status, and compare it to the stat value in coitem_mst before you build any logic on the mapping.
My sales order is stuck in Planned and will not ship. What is going on?

Almost certainly a credit hold. When a customer exceeds their credit limit, SyteLine saves the line as Planned instead of Ordered — and an order stuck in Planned never ships, because Planned demand is not committed. Check the customer's credit status and On Order Balance first; the status is the symptom, the credit position is the cause.
What is cust_po and where is it stored?

cust_po is the customer's PO number — their reference for the order. It lives on both co_mst (header) and coitem_mst (lines). When a customer calls asking about their PO number, you are matching against cust_po, not co_num, which is SyteLine's internal order number.
Walk me through the order-to-cash flow in SyteLine.

It starts with an estimate or quote; on a win, the estimate can generate the sales order and the work order together. Lines start Planned; moving to Ordered fires the credit check and updates On Order Balance. Then pick, pack, and ship — the packing slip and BOL — which reduces on-hand, and invoicing follows shipment. EDI mirrors the flow: inbound 850 for demand, 856 for the ASN, 810 for the invoice, 860 for changes.
Does shipping a customer order reduce on-hand inventory?

Yes. Pick/pack/ship is one of the reducers of on-hand, alongside job material issues, PO returns, stock adjustments, cycle counts, and physical-inventory postings. Every one of those movements lands in matltran, so the audit trail will show the shipment that took the quantity.
What are the EDI transaction sets SyteLine uses for order-to-cash?

Inbound: 850 is the demand or PO, 856 is the ASN (advance ship notice), 810 is the invoice, and 860 is the change. Outbound mirrors the same set. If a customer says they sent a change, you are looking for an 860 and checking whether it actually moved the order.
What are the job statuses in SyteLine?

Firm, Released, Complete, and History, plus Stopped to halt a job. A new job defaults to Firm. Released means it is authorized for shop-floor execution. Complete is set explicitly — the job does not close itself. History marks year-end purge candidates. And PLN is not a job status at all: it is a planned-order record from MRP or APS, and firming it converts it into a real job or PO.
What does it mean to firm a planned order?

Firming converts a PLN record — created by MRP or APS — into a real job or purchase order. Until it is firmed, a PLN is planning's suggestion, not an executable document: the shop floor cannot work it and purchasing cannot place it. If a job seems to exist but cannot release, check whether it is still sitting at PLN.
How do I close a job in SyteLine?

Explicitly: set Status to Complete on the Job Orders form, or complete the job through a job transaction. A job does not close itself as a side effect of receiving everything or finishing the work — close is an act, not a consequence. If a job looks done but is still open, nobody performed the close.
Why will my job not release?

Work the checklist: is it still a PLN record that was never firmed into a job? Is the BOM missing — the system normally prompts to copy the current BOM when you create a job without one? Is it a configurable item with an incomplete configuration, in which case the Status field stays disabled? One of those three is the blocker in nearly every case.
I created a job and SyteLine asked to copy the current BOM. Is something wrong?
No — that is normal. A new job with no BOM prompts you to copy the current BOM. It is the system being helpful, not an error. Accept the copy and keep going.
What does the Released status authorize on a job?

Released authorizes the job for shop-floor execution. Firm is the default for a new job — it exists but is not yet cleared to run. The Firm to Released transition is the handoff from planning to the floor, and labor, issues, and move transactions happen against Released jobs.
What is the Stopped job status for?

Stopped halts a job. It is the status you use when work must pause — a quality hold, a missing component, a priority change — without closing the job. The job stays in the system with its history intact and can be dispositioned later.
What does the History status mean on jobs and POs?

History marks records as purge candidates — for jobs, typically at year-end. It is the end of the lifecycle: Firm to Released to Complete to History on jobs, Planned to Ordered to Open to History on purchase orders. History is where records go to be archived, not worked.
What are the purchase order statuses?

Planned, Ordered, Open, then History for purge. A Planned PO is still in planning — no firm order exists. Ordered means it is ready to process. Do not confuse a Planned PO with a real commitment to the supplier; until it is Ordered, it is planning's draft.
What is the difference between a Planned PO and an Ordered PO?

A Planned PO is still in planning — it represents suggested supply, not a firm order, and you would not call the supplier about it. An Ordered PO is ready to process: it is a real commitment. MRP and APS create Planned POs; the buyer firms them into Ordered ones.
Does receiving a purchase order increase on-hand?

Yes — PO receipt increases on-hand, and PO returns reduce it. Both directions land in matltran. If on-hand jumped unexpectedly, check receipts first; if it dropped, check returns, shipments, issues, and adjustments — matltran will show which one it was.
Walk me through procure-to-pay in SyteLine.

It starts with requisitions, which become purchase orders — Planned while still in planning, Ordered when ready to process. Receipt increases on-hand; returns reduce it. The PO line statuses and the prom_date versus due_date fields are where delivery performance is measured, and matltran records every receipt and return.
What are the four steps of MRP in SyteLine?

One: plan independent demand — forecasts and customer orders. Two: net that demand against on-hand and scheduled receipts. Three: create planned orders for the net requirements. Four: explode the planned-order demand through the BOM into dependent component demand. Then the planner firms the resulting PLN orders into jobs or POs.
What does netting mean in MRP?

Netting means offsetting demand against what you already have or have coming: on-hand inventory and scheduled receipts. Only the net requirement — demand minus supply — becomes a planned order. If MRP suggests buying something you already have on the shelf, the netting step is where the investigation starts.
What is independent versus dependent demand?

Independent demand comes from outside the BOM: forecasts and customer orders. Dependent demand is derived — MRP explodes planned-order demand through the BOM to compute what components are needed. You plan independent demand; the system computes dependent demand from it.
What is the Order Action Report for?

It gives the planner reschedule and cancel guidance — which firm orders should move in, move out, or be cancelled based on the latest netting. When dates shift, the Order Action Report is the first thing a planner should read before touching anything manually.
What does the Net Change flag on an item do?

It limits replanning scope: with Net Change set, MRP only replans items whose demand or supply picture actually changed, instead of regenerating everything. It is how planners keep MRP runs fast and avoid churning firm orders that were fine.
How is APS different from MRP?

MRP nets demand and creates planned orders. APS goes further: it allocates on-hand and planned supply to demands by priority, with a supply-usage tolerance, and it can switch supply between demands — generating Move In and Move Out exception messages when it does. APS also controls PLN projected dates: they may change and are not user-editable the way firm dates are.
What are Move In and Move Out exception messages?

They are APS exceptions generated when the system switches supply between demands — pulling a planned receipt earlier (Move In) or pushing it later (Move Out) to serve higher-priority demand. If a PLN date moved and nobody touched it, check the APS exceptions before assuming user error.
Can I manually edit a PLN projected date that APS set?

No — APS controls PLN projected dates. They may change between runs and they are not user-editable the way firm dates are. If you need a different date, firm the PLN into a job or PO and manage the firm date, or address the underlying priority and supply picture that made APS choose the date.
What is supply-usage tolerance in APS?

It is the tolerance APS applies when allocating on-hand and planned supply to demands by priority. APS does not just net like MRP — it assigns supply to the highest-priority demands first, and the tolerance governs how aggressively it consumes shared supply. When a lower-priority demand loses its supply, the Move In/Move Out exceptions explain why.
Explain on-hand versus allocated versus available.

On-hand is physical quantity. Allocated is quantity reserved by open demand — order lines and job materials. Available, the ATP figure, is on-hand minus allocated as the standard convention, though exact bucket math varies by version and tenant, so treat the formula as the baseline, not your tenant's law. The diagnostic power is in the relationship: available tells you whether demand has already claimed the physical stock.
Available quantity went negative. Is the data wrong?

Not necessarily — read it by cause. If on-hand is non-negative and available is negative, allocated demand exceeds physical supply: that is the diagnostic signal, report it honestly and never clamp it. If on-hand itself is negative with little or no allocation, the negative comes from on-hand — check the On Hand Neg Flag and walk matltran for the item.
Can inventory go negative in SyteLine?

Explicitly yes, via the On Hand Neg Flag on the Inventory Parameters form — SyteLine allows it as a configured choice, and the exception list even includes Initial Quantity On Hand Negative. But there is a hard rule: on-hand serialized inventory cannot go negative. A negative on a serialized item is a data-integrity red flag, not a configuration choice.
What reduces on-hand inventory?

Job material issues, customer-order shipments, PO returns, stock adjustments, cycle counts, and physical-inventory postings. Every one of them lands in matltran. When on-hand drops unexpectedly, matltran tells you which of these six did it — never guess, read the transactions.
What is backflushing?

Backflushing auto-issues a job's materials when an operation or the job is completed, based on the completed quantity. The default is set at the item level but can be overridden per Job Materials record through the backflush and bflush_loc fields. Every backflushed issue lands in matltran like any other material transaction.
Where do I turn on lot tracking for an item?

On the Items form, Controls tab — Lot Track, enabled per item. An item can be both lot-tracked and serial-tracked at the same time. Lot numbers can be preassigned on a PO, a transfer order line, a job, or a co-job, and preassigned lots stay allocated and unusable until the source document is Complete.
What does it mean for a lot to be preassigned?

The lot number is reserved against a specific source — a PO, transfer order line, job, or co-job — before the material physically exists. Preassigned lots stay allocated and unusable for anything else until the source is Complete. If a lot shows on-hand but cannot be picked, check whether it is preassigned to an open source.
Why is my inventory negative? Walk me through the diagnosis.

First check the On Hand Neg Flag on the Inventory Parameters form — negatives may be allowed by configuration. Then pull matltran for the item and look for the usual causes: ship-before-receipt timing, backflush over-reporting from overstated completed quantities, duplicate issues, or adjustments. If the item is serialized, stop treating it as a timing issue — serialized on-hand cannot go negative, so that is a data-integrity red flag.
What is the credit hold and how does it show up?

When a customer exceeds their credit limit, SyteLine saves the order line as Planned instead of Ordered. There is no big red error — the hold expresses itself as a status. The line will not credit-check, will not update On Order Balance, and will never ship until the credit position is resolved. In multi-site, the originating site controls the order's credit-hold status, and On Order Balance is cumulative across replicating sites.
In a multi-site tenant, which site controls credit hold on an order?

The originating site controls the order's credit-hold status. On Order Balance itself is cumulative across the replicating sites, so a customer can be fine at one site and over limit in total. When credit behavior looks inconsistent across sites, check where the order originated.
What is the formula for Variable Labor Overhead?

Total hours times the Var Lbr Ovhd Rate. Fixed Labor Overhead is total hours times the Fix Lbr Ovhd Rate. The rates come from the Departments form or the job operation. Cost buckets are material, labor, and machine and labor overhead — and jobtran is the audit trail if the hours themselves are in question.
A job material has a scrap factor of 1.5. What does that mean?

The scrap factor is a multiplier of completed quantity: 1.5 means 50 percent more material is consumed than the BOM calls for. If the BOM says one unit per completed assembly, the system plans and issues one and a half. Check scrap_fact on jobmatl when material usage runs hot — the factor is often the explanation.
What are the cost buckets on a job?

Material, labor, and machine and labor overhead. Labor and overhead flow from reported hours through jobtran — variable overhead is total hours times the variable rate, fixed overhead is total hours times the fixed rate, with rates from the Departments form or the job operation. If job cost looks wrong, decompose it by bucket before theorizing.
Walk me through the manufacturing flow on a released job.

Operations are defined with setup and run standards, work center, resources, and cost rates; materials attach to operations. After release, labor is reported through Factory Track with Start Run, materials are issued, move transactions shift quantities between operations — and can receive completed quantity into a stockroom location — scrap is reported, the job receipt puts finished goods into inventory, and finally someone sets the status to Complete explicitly. Nothing closes itself.
What is a move transaction?

A move transaction shifts quantities between operations on a job as work progresses — and it can also receive completed quantity into a stockroom location. It is how the floor reports that work moved forward. Move transactions, issues, and completions together tell the story of where a job actually stands.
What is Factory Track?

Factory Track is the shop-floor labor reporting path — Start Run and the related transactions that record who worked on what, for how long. Those reported hours flow into jobtran and from there into labor and overhead costing. If labor cost is questioned, Factory Track activity and jobtran are the evidence.
Why is sales order 12345 late? Show me how you would investigate.

I would plan it in one line — trace the lines, check availability, then supply — and work it. First pull the order: header, open lines, promise_date and due_date, line statuses. For each open line, check item availability: if available is below the open quantity, the line is short. For short items, check open POs — prom_date versus today, quantity received versus ordered — and work orders: Released but not Complete means behind, PLN means not even firmed. For manufactured items, explode the BOM and check each component. And check the customer for credit hold, because an order stuck Planned never ships. Every claim I make traces to a record I actually pulled; anything I could not check, I say so plainly.
An order line is short on available quantity. What is the next step?

Check supply, in order: open purchase orders for the item — compare prom_date to today and quantity received to quantity ordered — and open work orders — Released but not Complete is behind schedule, PLN is not even firmed yet. The usual culprit is a late PO with no receipt, which makes the delay a supplier problem, not a shop-floor problem. For a manufactured item, explode the BOM and check each component's availability before concluding anything.
How do I tell whether a late order is a supplier problem or a shop-floor problem?

Look at the supply records. If PO-789 for the short item was due Tuesday, shows no receipt, and today is Friday, the supplier is three days late — that is a supplier problem, and no amount of shop-floor urgency fixes it. If instead the work order is Released but not Complete and components are available, the delay is on the floor. The records decide; do not guess.
The item is manufactured and we are short. What now?

Explode the BOM and check availability of each component, one by one. The parent being short usually means a component is short — check each component's on-hand, allocated, and available, then its own supply (POs and work orders). Work down the tree until you find the component with no coverage; that is where the delay lives.
All order lines show coverage but the order is still late. What else could it be?

Check credit hold first — an order stuck in Planned never ships no matter how much material is available. Then check the dates: promise_date and due_date are separate fields, and when promise_date is blank, due date is used. A line can be covered against the due date and still miss the promise date if someone conflated the two.
What is the difference between due_date, promise_date, and release_date on an order line?

Three separate fields on coitem_mst, never to be conflated. due_date is when it is due, promise_date is what was promised to the customer, release_date is the release date. When promise_date is blank, the due date is used. Late-against-which-date is always the first question in a delivery dispute.
A work order shows status Released but the job is not done. What does that tell me?

Released means authorized for shop-floor execution — work should be happening. Released but not Complete with the due date approaching means the job is behind. Check jobtran for reported labor, check material issues against jobmatl, and check move transactions to see how far the work actually progressed. If the work order is still PLN, it was never firmed — planning has not released it at all.
My job shows everything received but it is still open. Why?

Because close is an explicit act in SyteLine. Set Status to Complete on the Job Orders form, or complete the job through a job transaction. Receiving everything and finishing the work do not close the job by themselves — if nobody performed the close, the job stays open no matter how done it looks.
The Status field is disabled on my job. What is wrong?

For a configurable item with an incomplete configuration, the Status field stays disabled — that is one of the classic release blockers. Finish the configuration and the field enables. The other usual blockers are a PLN record that was never firmed into a job and a missing BOM.
What is an outside operation?

An outside operation is a routing step performed externally — sent to a supplier or subcontractor rather than done on your floor. It shows up in the routing with its own lead time and cost, and it is one of the places a job can silently wait: the operation is with the vendor, not in your building.
What is a phantom BOM?

A phantom BOM is a bill of material that does not create inventory — it is a grouping convenience that explodes through to its components when planned or issued. You will see the components move, never the phantom itself. Do not go looking for phantom part numbers in stock.
What is an ECN?

An ECN is an Engineering Change Notice — the controlled document that introduces a change to an item, BOM, or routing. It is the reason the BOM you see today is not the BOM from last month. When a build does not match expectations, check whether an ECN moved the revision under you.
What are alternate parts in SyteLine?

Alternate parts are approved substitutes for a BOM component — materials engineering has blessed them as interchangeable. They matter in shortages: when the primary component has no coverage, the alternate may. Availability analysis that ignores alternates can report a shortage that the floor could actually work around.
What is the difference between a co-product and a by-product?

Both come out of the same process, but a co-product is an intended output with real value while a by-product is incidental. The distinction drives costing and planning treatment — co-products share the cost model deliberately, by-products are accounted for as what they are: something that showed up alongside the real output.
What do JIT and kanban mean in the SyteLine context?

JIT and kanban are pull-based material flow methods — produce and move only what the next step actually needs. SyteLine tracks JIT activity alongside jobs and work centers, and jobtran records labor against JIT as well as jobs and production schedules. It is the opposite posture from building to a forecast and hoping.
What is kitting?

Kitting is staging a complete set of components as one package for a job or order — everything the floor needs, gathered and issued together. It front-loads the material hunt so the job does not stall mid-run waiting for a component nobody pulled.
What is the Material Planner Workbench?

It is the planner's working form — the place where demand, supply, and exceptions come together for day-to-day decisions. Paired with the Order Action Report's reschedule and cancel guidance and the Planning Detail views, it is where a planner lives most of the day.
What is the Demand Detail form for?

Demand Detail, including the Scheduler view, shows where demand is coming from — the orders, forecasts, and planned demands consuming supply. When available quantity looks wrong, Demand Detail shows you who allocated it.
What is the Shop Floor Control Parameters form?

It holds the shop-floor control settings for the site — the parameters that govern how jobs, labor reporting, and move transactions behave. When floor behavior seems off across many jobs, the parameters are worth checking before blaming individual transactions.
What are Production Schedules in SyteLine?

Production schedules are the repetitive-manufacturing planning construct — rate-based rather than order-based. jobtran records labor against production schedules as well as jobs, JIT, and work centers. If you build the same thing every day, schedules are the tool; if you build to discrete orders, jobs are.
What is a transfer order?

A transfer order moves material between sites or warehouses within the tenant. Lots can be preassigned on a transfer order line, and like other preassignments they stay allocated and unusable until the source is Complete. In multi-site work, transfer orders are the connective tissue between locations.
What is u_m on order and job material records?

u_m is the unit of measure — it appears on coitem_mst lines and on jobmatl records, among others. Quantity without a unit of measure is a number without meaning: always read qty_ordered with its u_m, especially when conversions are in play.
What is the BOL in the shipping flow?

The BOL — bill of lading — is the shipping document that travels with the freight. In the order-to-cash flow, pick and pack produce the shipment, the packing slip describes it, the BOL covers its transport, shipment reduces on-hand, and invoicing follows. The BOL is the carrier's receipt for what left your dock.
When does invoicing happen relative to shipment?

Invoicing follows shipment. The physical flow — pick, pack, ship with packing slip and BOL — reduces on-hand first; the invoice comes after. If an invoice exists without a shipment, or a shipment without an invoice, that gap is the thing to investigate.
An estimate just turned into an order. What should I expect in the system?

On a win, the estimate can generate the sales order and the work order together. Expect the order lines to start in Planned — they will not update On Order Balance or pass credit check until they move to Ordered. The work order side starts as a job at Firm, or as a PLN if it came through planning.
What does 850, 856, 810, 860 mean on the EDI side?

850 is the inbound demand or purchase order, 856 is the advance ship notice, 810 is the invoice, and 860 is the change — with outbound mirroring the same set. When a trading partner says they sent something, the set number tells you what kind of something it was and where in the flow to look.
Why do statuses matter so much in SyteLine? They look like labels.

They are not labels — they are load-bearing. The Scheduler and APS interpret transactions by status code: a Planned line is uncommitted demand, an Ordered line is committed and credit-checked, a Released job is cleared for the floor. Change a status and you change what the system does with the record. Treat every status as an instruction.
What is the Past Due pattern I should watch for on purchase orders?

Quantity ordered greater than quantity received, status O, and the due date in the past. It is a community-reported pattern, so verify the exact field semantics on your tenant — but when those three conditions hold, you are looking at a PO the supplier has not fulfilled. That is usually where a late order's story begins.
Should I ever invent an IDO or field name when answering a SyteLine question?

Never. Name real tables, fields, forms, and IDOs when they sharpen the answer; if you are unsure of an exact name, describe the concept and say the name should be confirmed on the tenant — against IdoCollections and IdoProperties. An invented name that looks plausible is worse than no name at all, because someone will build on it.
The tenant's data contradicts the knowledge pack. Which wins?

The tenant's live data wins, every time. The pack is the product baseline for versions 7.x through 10.x and up; tenant configuration — versions, custom fields, custom statuses — varies. Domain knowledge explains what records mean; it never substitutes for them. Reason from records, not from vibes.
What does reason from records, not from vibes mean in practice?

It means every factual claim about the tenant's data traces to a tool result — a record you actually pulled. Domain knowledge tells you what the records mean and where to look next, but it never manufactures facts. If a step cannot be checked, you say so plainly and mark the conclusion accordingly.
How should an agentic SyteLine investigation be structured?

State the plan in a line or two, then work it: chain dependent queries where each result shapes the next, within a bounded budget. Synthesize briefly with citations to real records — no raw table dumps, no invented entities, numbers, or statuses. End honest about gaps: anything unchecked is stated, not hidden. The diagnosis recommends; the human decides.
What is the Departments form used for?

Departments holds labor and overhead rates — the Var and Fix Lbr Ovhd Rates used in overhead costing — among other department-level settings. When job overhead looks wrong across many jobs, check whether the department rates changed before auditing individual job operations.
What is the difference between the Job Operations and Job Materials forms?

Job Operations holds the routing steps — setup and run standards, work center, resources, cost rates. Job Materials holds what gets consumed at those operations — item, quantities, scrap factor, backflush settings. Time is tracked against operations in jobtran; material is tracked against materials in matltran. Cost questions go to operations; shortage questions go to materials.
What is the Engineering Workbench?

The Engineering Workbench is where BOMs and routings are built and maintained — the engineering definition of how a product is made. Copy Routing and Copy BOM functions live nearby for reusing existing definitions. When the floor builds something different from what engineering defined, the workbench is the reference for what was supposed to happen.
What is the Lot/Serial Master?

The Lot/Serial Master is the master record for tracked lots and serial numbers — the identity registry for everything lot- or serial-tracked. Transactions move them, but the master defines them. Traceability questions start here.
Can one item be both lot-tracked and serial-tracked?

Yes — an item can be both. Lot tracking is enabled per item on the Items form, Controls tab, via Lot Track, and serial tracking can coexist with it. The Lot/Serial Master carries both identities. Do not assume one tracking method excludes the other.
Where does backflush get its default setting?

The default is set at the item level, and it can be overridden per Job Materials record through the backflush and bflush_loc fields. So two jobs for the same item can backflush differently if someone overrode the record. When backflushed quantities surprise you, check the jobmatl record — not just the item.
Completed quantity was overstated on a job. What breaks downstream?

Everything downstream of the completion: backflushing auto-issues material based on completed quantity, so overstated completion over-issues material — and every one of those issues lands in matltran, dragging on-hand down. It is one of the classic causes of negative inventory. Fix the completion reporting first, then true up the material.
What is the Material Transactions form?

It is the window into material movements — the form-side view of what matltran records. When you need to reconstruct what happened to an item's quantity, the Material Transactions form and matltran are the same story told two ways: the form for browsing, the table for the audit trail.
What is Material Allocation?

Material Allocation is the reservation side of inventory — open demand (order lines, job materials) holding claim against on-hand, which is exactly what allocated means in the on-hand versus allocated versus available math. When available is negative with healthy on-hand, the allocation view shows who claimed it.
How do I read a negative available quantity honestly?

Report it as-is and diagnose the cause: with non-negative on-hand, negative available means allocated demand exceeds physical supply — that is the signal, never clamp it to zero. With negative on-hand and little allocation, the negative comes from on-hand itself — check the Neg Flag and matltran. Clamping hides the exact information the planner needs.
A planner says MRP suggested buying something we already have. Where do I look?

Start at the netting step: MRP nets demand against on-hand and scheduled receipts, so a suggestion to buy what you hold means netting saw something you do not — allocated quantity holding the on-hand, a Net Change flag excluding the item from replanning, or scheduled receipts the planner forgot. Pull the item's on-hand, allocated, and scheduled receipts before concluding MRP is wrong.
What is bucket costing?

Bucket costing breaks product cost into buckets — material, labor, machine overhead, labor overhead — instead of one blended number. It is the vocabulary for answering which part of the cost moved: the buckets decompose a variance into something actionable.
An order line promised Tuesday but the PO arrives Thursday. What is the diagnosis?

The line is short because of the supplier, not the floor. The diagnostic chain: line short on available, open PO with prom_date Thursday against a Tuesday promise_date, no receipt yet — the supplier is two days late. Report it as a supply delay with the PO as evidence, and note the promise_date versus due_date distinction if anyone conflates them.
The work order is at PLN and the order is late. What do I tell the customer?

Tell them the truth the records show: the work order was never firmed — PLN is a planning record, not a job — so production never had an executable document. The delay is in planning release, not on the floor. The fix is firming the PLN into a job, and the honest status is that manufacturing has not started.
How do blanket order lines differ from regular lines?

Blanket lines are releases against a long-term agreement rather than one-shot demand, but their lifecycle is the same: Planned, Ordered, Complete. The same rules apply — Planned does not update On Order Balance, Ordered fires the credit check. The blanket is the umbrella; each release line lives the normal lifecycle underneath it.
What is the Job Bill of Material form?

The Job Bill of Material is the BOM as attached to a specific job — the engineering BOM copied or referenced at job creation, which the job then owns. If the engineering BOM changed after the job was created, the job's BOM may differ from the current revision — and the job builds to its own copy, not the latest.
The job built to a different BOM than engineering's current one. Is that a bug?

Usually not — the job owns its BOM copy from creation time. If an ECN moved the engineering revision after the job was created, the job still builds to what it was given. Compare the Job Bill of Material against the current engineering revision and check ECN history before calling it wrong.
What is a rework job?

A rework job is a job created to fix or reprocess existing material — bringing nonconforming or damaged goods back to spec. It consumes labor and possibly material like any job, and its transactions land in the same audit trails: jobtran for labor, matltran for material.
What is an estimate job?

An estimate job is the work-order side of an estimate — when an estimate wins, it can generate the sales order and the work order together. The estimate job is the planning seed that becomes a real Firm job. If the estimate job never converted, there is no executable work document downstream.
Where do overhead rates come from — the department or the job operation?

Either: rates come from the Departments form or from the job operation itself. The operation can carry its own rates, which override the department default. When one job's overhead looks out of line with its siblings, check whether its operation carries custom rates.
What is the Location Inventory Detail form?

It shows inventory broken down by location — the where behind the on-hand number. Item-level on-hand is an aggregate; Location Inventory Detail decomposes it. When the total looks right but the floor cannot find the stock, the location detail usually reveals it sitting somewhere unexpected.
What are Purchase Order Requisitions?

Requisitions are the request stage before a PO exists — someone asks purchasing to buy something. They convert into purchase orders, which then live the Planned to Ordered to Open lifecycle. A requisition is intent; a PO is commitment.
The customer changed their PO. What EDI document is that and what should I check?

That is an 860, the change transaction. Check whether it actually moved the order: compare the order's current lines and dates against what the 860 requested. An 860 received is not an 860 applied — confirm the change landed before telling the customer it is handled.
What is the ASN in the EDI flow?

The ASN — advance ship notice, the 856 — tells the customer what is coming before it arrives. In the order-to-cash EDI mirror, the 850 brought the demand, the 856 announces the shipment, the 810 invoices it. If the customer says they never got notice, the 856 is the document to trace.
Why would a line be saved as Planned when the CSR swears they ordered it?

Credit hold is the usual answer: exceeding the credit limit saves the line as Planned instead of Ordered, silently. The CSR did everything right and the system quietly refused to commit. Check the customer's credit position and On Order Balance — the status is the system telling you what happened, if you know how to read it.
What is the Vendors form for in a diagnostics context?

Vendors is the supplier master — the other side of every PO conversation. When a PO is late, the vendor record gives you the contact and the delivery history to pair with the poitem_mst facts: prom_date versus today, quantity received versus ordered. The diagnosis comes from the PO records; the vendor form tells you who to call about it.
What is the Customers form the master of?

The Customers form is the customer master — credit limit, terms, and the standing data behind every order. Credit-hold diagnosis starts here: the limit on the customer record against the cumulative On Order Balance is the comparison that decides whether a line stays Planned.
What is the Items form the master of?

The Items form is the item master — the global definition: description, units, costing, and the Controls tab where Lot Track is enabled per item. The per-site side lives in itemwhse on the Item Warehouses form. Global definition on Items, site reality on Item Warehouses.
What is the Item Warehouses form for?

Item Warehouses maintains the itemwhse records — the per-site side of each item: quantities, planning parameters, costing at the site level. Availability questions are answered here, not on the global item master, because on-hand and allocated live per site.
What is the Job Transactions form?

Job Transactions is the form-side view of job activity — completions, labor, and material movements against jobs, feeding jobtran and matltran. When a job's status and its reality disagree, the transactions form shows what was actually reported.
What are Copy Routing and Copy BOM used for?

They reuse existing engineering definitions when creating similar items or jobs — copy the routing, copy the BOM, adjust the differences. It is also what the system offers when you create a job with no BOM: copy the current BOM. Reuse beats retyping, and it keeps definitions consistent.
How should a planner use the Order Action Report day to day?

Read it before touching firm orders: it gives reschedule and cancel guidance from the latest netting — which orders should move in, move out, or be cancelled. Manual date changes made without reading it tend to fight the next MRP or APS run. The report is planning telling you what it already figured out.
What is Planning Detail?

Planning Detail is the detailed planning view — the demand and supply picture behind the summary numbers. When a planned order's quantity or date surprises you, Planning Detail shows the netting that produced it: the demands, the on-hand, the scheduled receipts, and the arithmetic between them.
What is a co-job?

A co-job is a job linked to a customer order — production tied directly to the demand that created it. Lots can be preassigned on a co-job, and like all preassignments they stay allocated and unusable until the source is Complete. The co-job is the thread connecting the sales order to the shop floor.
What are Production Schedule Items?

Production Schedule Items are the line-level detail of production schedules — the repetitive-manufacturing equivalent of job records. Labor reported against them lands in jobtran alongside job, JIT, and work-center activity. Rate-based building is planned here, not in discrete jobs.
An order is late and the component PO shows partial receipt. How do I read that?

Compare quantity received against qty_ordered_conf on the poitem_mst line: partial receipt means some supply exists but not all. The open quantity — ordered minus received — is what is still missing, and prom_date versus today tells you how late the balance is. A partial receipt splits the diagnosis: cover what arrived, expedite the balance, and give the customer the honest partial picture.
Two demands need the same planned supply. Who wins?

Under APS, the higher-priority demand wins — APS allocates on-hand and planned supply to demands by priority, with a supply-usage tolerance. The loser generates Move In or Move Out exceptions when its supply gets reassigned. Priority is not a suggestion in APS; it is the allocation rule.
A PLN date moved overnight and nobody touched it. What happened?

APS moved it. PLN projected dates are controlled by APS — they change between runs and are not user-editable like firm dates. Check the APS exception messages for Move In or Move Out activity against that demand: the system reallocated supply by priority, and the date followed the supply.
What is the scope of the knowledge pack you reason from?

Generic product knowledge for SyteLine, versions 7.x through 10.x and up — no tenant data. It is the baseline I reason from, but the tenant's live data and IdoCollections are ground truth. Behavior varies by version and configuration, and IDO names marked verify are community-corroborated, so I confirm them on the tenant rather than asserting them.
A user asks about a table I have never heard of. How do I respond?

Describe the concept they are after using the tables and fields I do know, and say the exact name should be confirmed on the tenant. Never invent a table or field name — a plausible-sounding invented name will send someone digging through a schema for something that does not exist.
Why is firming discipline important for planners?

Because until a PLN is firmed, nothing downstream can act on it: the floor cannot work a plan, purchasing cannot place a planned PO, and dates stay under APS control. Unfirmed PLNs are the most common invisible delay — everything looks planned and nothing is executable. Firming is the moment planning becomes commitment.
What is the relationship between forecasts and MRP?

Forecasts are independent demand — step one of MRP plans them alongside customer orders. MRP nets that demand against on-hand and scheduled receipts, creates planned orders for the net, and explodes through the BOM. A bad forecast does not just miss sales; it manufactures the wrong components.
How do I explain ATP to a salesperson?

On-hand is what is physically here. Allocated is what is already promised to other orders and jobs. Available is what is left for you — on-hand minus allocated, as the standard convention. If available covers the order, promise it; if not, the shortfall is either a supply problem or a priority problem, and I can trace which.
What is the most common root cause when a manufactured order is late?

A late purchased component, not the shop floor. The veteran's checklist runs: open lines and dates, item availability, then supply — and supply usually shows a PO with a prom_date in the past and no receipt. Explode the BOM and check each component before blaming production; the floor can only build with what purchasing delivered.
What should I check before promising a customer a date?

The line's promise_date versus due_date — they are separate fields, and blank promise_date means due date is used. Then availability: available below the open quantity means short. Then supply coverage for the shortfall: POs with prom_dates and work orders with statuses. Promise from the records, not from optimism.
A cycle count adjusted on-hand down sharply. What now?

Treat the adjustment as a fact and re-derive: the count says the physical stock was overstated, and matltran shows what the system thought happened. Recompute available — on-hand minus allocated — because every promise made against the old on-hand is now suspect. Then find why the system drifted: missed issues, unreported scrap, or ship-before-receipt timing are the usual suspects.
What does it mean that application event handlers hold business-process logic?

It means the workflow rules — what happens when a status changes, what validations fire, what cascading updates run — live in event handlers attached to the application, not in the form layout and not in the database. When behavior differs from what the fields suggest, the event handlers are where the real logic executed.
Why keep custom metadata separate from the base application?

So upgrades do not destroy it. The base application ships from the vendor; your customizations live as separate metadata, and FormSync merges the two at upgrade time. Mix them and every upgrade becomes a rewrite; keep them separate and upgrades become a merge.
What is OpenSession for on the IDO runtime?

OpenSession establishes the session context for IDO runtime calls — the identity and context under which LoadCollection, UpdateCollection, and Invoke execute. Business rules and security evaluate within that session, which is why the same IDO call can behave differently for different users.
Summarize the veteran's checklist for a late sales order in one pass.

Pull the order: open lines, promise_date and due_date, statuses. For each open line check availability — available below open quantity is short. For short items check open POs (prom_date versus today, received versus ordered) and work orders (Released not Complete is behind; PLN is not firmed). For manufactured items explode the BOM per component. Check credit hold — Planned never ships. Cite the records for every claim, state what you could not check, and name the root cause only when the evidence supports it.
Summarize the veteran's checklist for negative inventory in one pass.

Check the On Hand Neg Flag — negatives may be configured. Then walk matltran for the item: ship-before-receipt timing, backflush over-reporting from overstated completions, duplicate issues, adjustments. If the item is serialized, treat it as a data-integrity red flag, because serialized on-hand cannot go negative. Report the cause you find, not the cause you expected.
Summarize the veteran's checklist for a job that will not release or close.

For release: still at PLN (firm it), missing BOM (accept the copy prompt), or incomplete configuration on a configurable item (Status stays disabled). For close: remember it is explicit — set Complete on the Job Orders form or complete via a job transaction; finishing the work never closes the job by itself. Status blockers first, explicit actions second.
What is the single most important habit for agentic SyteLine diagnostics?

Let each query's result shape the next one, and cite the records. Plan in a line or two, pull the order, follow the evidence through lines to availability to supply to BOM components, and never assert what you did not retrieve. The habit is not knowing the answer — it is knowing the next query.
A new planner asks where to start learning SyteLine. What do you tell them?

Learn the lifecycles first: order lines Planned to Ordered to Complete, jobs Firm to Released to Complete, POs Planned to Ordered to Open — statuses are load-bearing. Then the tables behind them: co_mst and coitem_mst, po_mst and poitem_mst, job and jobmatl, and matltran as the audit trail for everything. Then MRP's four steps and what APS adds. Everything else — forms, EDI, costing — hangs off that skeleton.
